hook.text: A microphone near a speaker screams louder and louder. The output feeds back into the input. Runaway loop.

buildup.text: A feedback loop occurs when the result of a process becomes its own input, amplifying or dampening it.

discovery.text: Positive loops amplify: panic selling crashes prices, causing more panic. Negative loops stabilize: a thermostat.

twist.text: Systems with no negative feedback loops tend to explode or collapse. Balance requires a braking force.

climax.text: Social media algorithms are positive loops: engagement breeds more of what triggered engagement.

punchline.text: Loops can build you up or tear you down.

quiz.question: What is the difference between positive and negative feedback loops?
options: Positive is good, negative is bad

details.summary: Feedback loops occur when a system's output circles back as input, either amplifying change through positive feedback or dampening it through negative feedback. Understanding these loops explains exponential growth, market bubbles, temperature regulation, and countless natural and social phenomena.
details.whyItMatters: Most people think linearly, but the world runs on feedback loops. Recognizing them helps you predict when systems will accelerate, stabilize, or crash.
takeaways: Positive feedback amplifies change; negative feedback stabilizes
Exponential growth is driven by positive feedback loops
Most complex systems contain multiple interacting feedback loops

faq.question: What is the difference between positive and negative feedback?
faq.answer: Positive feedback reinforces the direction of change, creating acceleration. Negative feedback opposes the direction, creating stability. A microphone squeal is positive feedback. A thermostat is negative feedback. Neither positive nor negative means good or bad in this context.

faq.question: Why do feedback loops cause surprises?
faq.answer: Because humans think linearly. A positive feedback loop starts slowly and then explodes exponentially. By the time you notice the acceleration, the system may be past the point of easy correction. This is why bubbles, pandemics, and viral content all feel sudden.
